notes.meaning: "The Word" is a name for Jesus, God's Son. Our words show others what is in our minds, and in the same way Jesus shows us the mind of God. He already existed when everything else began, so he has always been. "With God" shows he is a distinct person from the Father. "Was God" shows he is truly God himself, not a lesser being.

John repeats himself on purpose, so no one can miss it. The Word did not start being with God at some point in time. He was with God from before time began. This closeness between Father and Son has always been.

Everything that exists was made through Jesus, from the highest angel to the smallest worm. Nothing is left out. Only God can create, so this shows Jesus is God. It also means the one who made us is well able to save us.

Jesus is the source of every living thing's life, and he keeps it going. People were given something more as well: the light of understanding and reason, which sets us apart from animals. Barnes adds that Jesus is also the source of spiritual life for souls that are dead in sin.

Because of sin, the world and the human heart are full of darkness. Yet Christ's light keeps on shining. Most people did not take the light in. They refused and rejected it. But the darkness could not overpower it or put it out either.
Here John the Baptist is introduced. Jesus was called God, but John is called a man. He was a great man, but still only a man. What gave him authority was that God sent him as his messenger.

John's whole job was to be a witness and point people to Jesus, the Light. The goal was for people to believe in Christ through John's message, not to believe in John. He woke people up to their sin so they would be ready to welcome Jesus.

However bright John was, he was not the Light himself. Some people looked so hard at John that they missed Christ, as later happened with some believers at Ephesus. The lesson is not to think too highly of church leaders. They point to the Light, but they are not the Light.
Jesus is the true Light. He shines by his own power and borrows light from no one. All the real light any person has comes from him. It is not just for one nation but for people everywhere.

differ.view: This light reaches every person as conscience, a sense of right and wrong. It is graciously given by Christ to show people their sin, and if people did not resist it, it would grow brighter and brighter.
This verse speaks only of the common light of reason and conscience that all people have. It is not saving grace offered equally to everyone. Only God's Spirit opens heaven to those he has chosen.

notes.meaning: Jesus came into the very world he had made. He walked on his own ground and breathed his own air. Yet the world did not recognize or welcome its own Maker. He did not come in the outward splendor people expected.

"His own" means the people of Israel, whom God had chosen as his special people. They had the Scriptures that told them to expect him. Even so, most of them would not welcome him as the Messiah, God's promised king.

Some people did welcome Jesus, which means they trusted in him. He gave them the right to become God's children. This new birth does not come from family line, so being born a child of Abraham was not enough. It also does not come from human effort or choice. It is God's own work in the heart.

differ.view: No one can believe unless God has first given them new birth. Faith itself flows from this new birth, and it is God's gift from heaven.
The moment people believe, they become God's children. Then God sends the Spirit of his Son into their hearts, so they cry out, "Father."

notes.meaning: God the Son became a real human being, weak and able to die like us, while staying fully God. "Made his dwelling" means he pitched his tent among us. This recalls the tabernacle, the worship tent where God's glory lived in Israel's camp. His disciples saw his glory in his miracles, his teaching, his goodness and his transfiguration, when his appearance shone with heavenly light. He was full of grace (God's kindness we don't deserve) and truth.

John began preaching before Jesus did, so Jesus came "after" him. Yet Jesus ranks far above John, because he existed long before John was born. In fact, he has always existed. John gladly gave Jesus first place.

Jesus overflows with grace, and every believer draws from that supply. "Grace upon grace" means one blessing piled on another, given over and over. We have nothing good that we did not receive from him. And there is nothing we need that he cannot give.

God's law came through Moses. It is holy and good, but it cannot give pardon or strength. It shows us our sin and holds shadows that picture what was coming. Jesus brings the real thing: grace that forgives and changes us, and the truth those shadows pointed to.

No one has ever seen God or known him fully. Even Moses could not see his face. Jesus is "at the Father's side," sharing his deepest love and his secret plans. So he alone can show us clearly what God is like.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Older translations say "the only begotten Son" here. Robertson says the best old manuscripts read "God only begotten" instead, which is the basis for the BSB's "who is Himself God."

notes.meaning: The Jewish leaders in Jerusalem sent priests and Levites to question John. These leaders were probably the great ruling council, called the Sanhedrin. Crowds were wondering whether John might be the Messiah, so the leaders wanted to know who he claimed to be.

John answered plainly and firmly: "I am not the Christ" (the Messiah, God's promised king). Many were ready to follow him, and he could have drawn a crowd. He refused to take honor that belonged to Jesus. This shows he was honest, not a fake.

People expected the prophet Elijah to come back in person before the Messiah. John said he was not Elijah in that sense, though he came in Elijah's spirit and power, as Jesus later said. He also was not "the Prophet" Moses had promised (Deuteronomy 18:15). John saw himself only as Christ's herald.
The messengers had to take an answer back to the leaders who sent them, so they pressed him. They wanted John to say plainly who he was. They trusted he would give an honest, direct reply.

John answered with words from Isaiah 40:3. He called himself only a "voice," which is a humble way to describe himself. His job was to cry out and get people ready for the Lord, like workers clearing a road before a king arrives.

The Pharisees were strict keepers of religious customs. Jews already baptized outsiders who joined their faith, but John was baptizing Jews too. The Pharisees thought only the Messiah, Elijah or the Prophet had the authority to start something like that. So they asked John why he was doing it.

John said he only gave the outward sign with water. The real power belongs to Christ. Then he startled them: the one they were waiting for was already standing among them, unnoticed. God is often nearer than we realize.
